classification.difficultyReason: Form general similarity proofs from midpoint ratios and parallel angles, then transfer the established midpoint result to triangles formed by the explicitly requested diagonals to prove both opposite-side pairs parallel.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Prove that: The line interval joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and half its length.

answer.short: The midpoint interval is parallel to the third side and half its length, by SAS similarity.
answer.worked:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be the midpoints of $AB$ and $BC$ in triangle $ABC$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{BX}{BA}&=\frac12\\\frac{BY}{BC}&=\frac12\end{align*}$$
Also $\angle XBY=\angle ABC$ (common angle). Therefore $\triangle XBY\sim\triangle ABC$ (SAS). Matching sides give $XY=\frac12AC$. Matching angles give $\angle BXY=\angle BAC$, so $XY\parallel AC$ (equal corresponding angles).

spec.description: Labelled triangle and midpoint interval supporting the proof.
spec.mathematics: X and Y are midpoints of AB and BC.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Prove that: The line through the midpoint of one side of a triangle parallel to another side of the triangle meets the third side at its midpoint.

answer.short: The third side is bisected, by AAA similarity.
answer.worked:
In triangle $ABC$, let $X$ be the midpoint of $AB$. Let the line through $X$ parallel to $AC$ meet $BC$ at $Y$. Then $\angle BXY=\angle BAC$ (corresponding angles) and $\angle XBY=\angle ABC$ (common angle). Thus $\triangle XBY\sim\triangle ABC$ (AAA).
$$\begin{align*}\frac{BY}{BC}&=\frac{BX}{BA}\\\frac{BY}{BC}&=\frac12\\BY&=\frac12BC\end{align*}$$
Therefore $BY=YC$, so $Y$ is the midpoint of $BC$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Prove that: The midpoints of the sides of a quadrilateral form the vertices of a parallelogram. Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral, and let $P$, $Q$, $R$ and $S$ be the midpoints of the sides $AB$, $BC$, $CD$ and $DA$ respectively. Construct diagonals $AC$ and $BD$.

answer.short: $PQ\parallel SR$ and $PS\parallel QR$; therefore $PQRS$ is a parallelogram.
answer.worked: Construct $AC$ and $BD$. In triangles $ABC$ and $ADC$, the midpoint theorem gives $PQ\parallel AC$ and $SR\parallel AC$. Hence $PQ\parallel SR$. In triangles $ABD$ and $BCD$, the midpoint theorem gives $PS\parallel BD$ and $QR\parallel BD$. Hence $PS\parallel QR$. Both pairs of opposite sides of $PQRS$ are parallel, so $PQRS$ is a parallelogram.

spec.description: An illustrative quadrilateral, four side midpoints, their connecting intervals and both diagonals.
spec.mathematics: P,Q,R,S bisect AB,BC,CD,DA respectively; AC and BD are construction diagonals.
spec.answerVisibility: Solution only; the student receives blank construction space.
